podcast.body: Dreampop, a genre that emerged in the 1980s, is noted as having a definite connection to Bedroom Pop, indicating a shared aesthetic or influence on the later genre. "And there's a definite connection to both Dreampop, which was a product of the 80s"

podcast.title: 21st Century Revival and Technology (2000s)
podcast.body: Dreampop, and its cousin Shoegaze, experienced a significant revival in the 21st century, partly driven by technological advancements. Laptops made it easier for artists to create densely textured, studio-quality music in bedrooms using synthesizers and software, facilitating a surge of new material by the time streaming services like Spotify launched in 2008.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Atmospheric and Textured Sound
podcast.body: Dreampop is fundamentally defined by its emphasis on creating atmosphere and rich textures, heavily utilizing reverb and echo effects. While related to Tweetpop, it typically conveys a slightly more serious attitude and often has a greater volume. The genre encompasses artists like the Cocteau Twins and Mazzy Star, known for their quiet sounds, but can also extend into the shoegaze realm with groups such as Slowdive and My Bloody Valentine. "Dreampop is all about atmosphere and textures with lots of reverb and echo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: COVID-19 Influence (2020s)
podcast.body: Dreampop made significant inroads in the 2020s, potentially due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Lockdown conditions encouraged many artists to create music in their bedrooms, increasing the supply of this type of music. Additionally, the genre's relaxing qualities offered a needed antidote to the stress and isolation of the time.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Characteristics
podcast.body: Defined by atmosphere, sonic textures, and sometimes sheer volume, Dreampop maintains a melodic core. It ranges in volume from barely audible softness to extreme loudness. Its history traces back to the immersive sounds of the 1960s, like The Velvet Underground, and the "Wall of Sound" techniques of Phil Spector.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Characteristics and Influence
podcast.body: Dreampop emerged by blending ideas from psychedelic music with intricate textures and atmospheric sounds, often achieved through electronics or studio techniques. The genre aimed for "total immersion in music," with acts like the Cocteau Twins pioneering a "dreamy, slightly stone sort of sound" and unique vocal approaches. "These groups copped ideas from psychedelic music and blended them with interesting textures and atmosphere, often using electronics or studio tricks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Coined by Alex Ayuli (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: The term "Dreampop" itself was coined by Alex Ayuli of AR Kane around the late 1980s. He used it as a way to define his band's sound and push back against journalists applying unwanted labels.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercial Licensing
podcast.body: Dreampop bands like Lush began licensing their music for TV advertisements, such as for the Volkswagen Passat in 1996, indicating the increasing prevalence of such deals across various genres. "In 1996, a song by the Dreampop band Lush ended up in a TV ad for the Volkswagen Passat."

podcast.title: Disputed Relationship with Shoegaze
podcast.body: There is a notable dispute among critics and music lovers about whether dreampop and shoegaze are the same genre, two distinct genres, or two facets of a single musical movement, without a definitive official answer. "hay mucha disputa entre el sugeis y el dreampop... al margen de interpretaciones porque no tenemos claro y no hay una uniformidad en si el sugeis y el dreampop son lo mismo o no son lo mismo."

podcast.title: Dreampop – Coined by Alex Elluley of AR Kane; Atmospheric, Textured; Lana Del Rey as Minimalist Example
podcast.body: Dreampop is a very atmospheric and highly textured form of alt rock with DNA from certain corners of Goth and psychedelic music. The term was apparently coined by Alex Elluley, part of an experimental British band from the mid-1980s called AR Kane. The sound is meant to immerse the listener in mood and vibe — often highly produced with effects-laden guitars and synths, or achieved through a special kind of minimalism. Dreampop often features breathy vocals, male or female. Lana Del Rey's 2012 work is cited as minimalist Dreampop. "As far as we can tell, the term Dreampop was coined by a guy named Alex Elluley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: European Focus
podcast.body: The cleaner, synthesizer-driven sound of dreampop gained significant focus in Europe and the United Kingdom. "que yo creo que sí focalizó mucho más en la parte europea y en la parte del reino unido."

podcast.title: Geographical Naming Convention
podcast.body: Some critics suggest that dreampop and shoegaze are the same movement but had different regional names. Dreampop was more commonly used in Europe and the United Kingdom, whereas shoegaze was prevalent in the United States and the Americas. "en Europa nunca casi nunca se usó la nomenclatura de sugeis, casi siempre se le llamó dreampop si ungeis era un nombre que se usaba mucho en los Estados Unidos y en América en general... y el dreampop era una nomenclatura que se usaba muy poco entonces hay críticos que consideran que es el mismo movimiento que en Estados Unidos y en América en general en Europa tenían como nombres distintos."

podcast.title: Goth Influence (Late 70s)
podcast.body: The emergence of Goth music in 1978-1979, characterized by an ethereal, spooky, dark, and minor-key feel, was a necessary precursor for proper Dreampop to form. This style, sometimes called ethereal wave or ethereal Goth, later morphed into something distinct but related to Dreampop.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heyday and Decline (Late 80s to Mid 90s)
podcast.body: The heyday of Dreampop extended from the late 1980s through to the mid-1990s. It was subsequently overshadowed by other 90s genres like Madchester, Britpop, Grunge, and the punk rock revival, receding to the margins but never entirely disappearing.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 1980s Characteristics
podcast.body: In the late 1980s, Dreampop was characterized by a dominance of female vocalists (though males also featured), breathy and quiet vocals, and a hazy, blurry mood. It was often associated with relaxation and a mind-blanking state, and could be enhanced by "recreational chemicals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legacy and Integration
podcast.body: Dreampop left a more profound legacy, integrating deeply into the Britpop movement of the 90s and expanding into the indie and independent music scenes. It also blended with electronic music, influenced by ambient artists, giving rise to an "electronic synthesizer dreampop" sound that has transcended and remains visible today through bands like The xx, Chromatics, The War on Drugs, and Radiohead. "el dreampop sí que era mejor dejaría una estela más profunda porque el dreampop se incorporó mucho a lo que seguía el britpop de los 90, se adentro mucho en lo que se gara rama más indie, más independiente tenemos también esa rama apasionante que se mezcló un poco con el electrónica porque teníamos esa influencia de Brian N, no de ella Michelle Jar, y nos dejaría ese dreampop electrónico desintetizador que era una pasada... y a día de hoy eso es un sonido que ha trascendido."

podcast.title: Origins in Early 80s
podcast.body: Dreampop emerged from the post-punk era in the early 1980s, influenced by the experimentation and new electronic technologies of the time, such as synthesizers, drum machines, and samplers. It has had a profound and lasting effect on music.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overlap with Sub-genres
podcast.body: Dreampop significantly touches on and overlaps with other alternative rock sub-genres, including shoegaze and modern psychedelic material.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sound Characteristics
podcast.body: Dreampop is characterized by a cleaner, less saturated sound, with lyrics that are much more intelligible. It is often more ambient, drawing influences from artists like Brian Eno and Jean-Michel Jarre, creating a romantic, ethereal, and melancholic atmosphere. It tends to utilize synthesizers more than guitar pedals, resulting in its distinct clean sound. "era un sonido como más limpio, un poco menos saturado, la letra se entendía mucho mejor, era más ambiental, teníamos influencias no tanto de sonidjuz pero sí de Braia Neno y de Yamis El Yard y de toda esta parte como más de música ambiental o que generaba como un pequeño ahí como un aura de sonido tan romántica y tan del espacio y que nos llamaba como música como más triste, más intimista, como más intelectual a veces, a lo mejor el dreampop no usaba tanto pedal de guitarra y usaba más sintetizador y lo cual le daba ese sonido más limpio y ese sonido."

"es una parte interesante de la primera etapa de Spiritualized cuando se iba cercando más al Dreampop."

podcast.title: UK Origins and US Expansion
podcast.body: Early Dreampop was primarily confined to the UK. However, American artists and collaborators like David Lynch, Angelo Badalamenti, and Julee Cruise, and bands like Galaxie 500, soon began exploring the genre's territory.

podcast.title: Volume Continuum
podcast.body: The genre's volume range is vast, spanning from "barely there softness" to an intensity "beyond a jet engine," yet it consistently retains a melodic quality.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Witchhouse Influence
podcast.body: Dreampop, along with Shoegaze, influenced Witchhouse, providing ethereal textures and characteristics of a "wall of sound." "y del Dreampop y el sugeys, tomó las texturas etéreas y son muro de sonido."
